summary:
EarthPulse is a free web tool that finds where rainfall, soil moisture, temperature and vegetation are changing around the world, and how sure we can be. It tests 627 land locations and 21 regions over 1981–2025 using NASA Earth observation data.

To be a trend detective, EarthPulse treats every apparent trend as a claim to test. It corrects for chance results from testing many places and for runs of similar years, then checks rainfall and temperature against a second independent dataset. Of 233 rainfall “trends” a simple test finds, only 114 survive. Each discovery answers four separate questions: is it significant, are the data reliable, is it confirmed independently, and is it large enough to matter.

Users can explore a world map of opposite trends, see unusual months, or simply ask a question by text or voice. The spoken answer highlights the matching places on the map.

Climate data is easy to misread. EarthPulse helps students, journalists and planners see what changed, how sure we are, and what the data cannot show.
details:
What it does and how it works

EarthPulse is a free web tool that finds where rainfall, soil moisture, temperature and vegetation are changing around the world, by how much, and how sure we can be. It tests 627 land locations on a global 5° grid, plus 21 named regions, using monthly NASA data from 1981 to 2025.

Every place goes through the same five steps:

  • Read: the data comes from NASA POWER (MERRA-2) and MODIS.
  • Test: a Mann-Kendall test, corrected for runs of similar years, with a Theil-Sen trend slope.
  • Correct: a check against chance results from testing 627 places at once, plus checks for abrupt jumps and for trends that flip when the first or last years are dropped.
  • Confirm: the same test on a second, independent dataset (GPCP for rainfall, NASA GISTEMP for temperature).
  • Explain: four separate evidence answers. Is it significant? Are the data reliable? Is it confirmed independently? Is it large enough to matter?

Users can:

  • browse a discovery feed with a printable evidence page for every result;
  • use the Opposite Trend Finder to see places where the same variable rises in one location and falls in another;
  • see several variables changing together at one place;
  • find unusual months, checked against a second dataset;
  • ask questions in plain English, by text or by voice. “Talk to EarthPulse” reads the answer aloud and highlights the place being described on the map and in the table.

Benefits

  • Honest confidence: every result says how sure it is and what it cannot show. Of 233 rainfall “trends” a simple test finds, only 114 survive the corrections, and EarthPulse shows that difference instead of hiding it.
  • Traceable: every number traces to open NASA data and a stated statistical test.
  • Easy to use: free, no login, works on a phone, and can be used by voice.

Intended impact

Students, journalists, teachers and local planners can check climate claims, and screen places before a deeper study, without misreading noise as a trend. It is a learning and screening tool. It is not a forecast and does not replace local studies.

Tools

  • Code: TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL and Recharts, hosted on Vercel.
  • Voice: the browser’s built-in speech recognition and speech output.
  • Statistics: written by the team, with 121 automated tests.
  • Optional AI: Google Gemini can reword explanations. It never computes anything: every number it writes is checked against EarthPulse’s results before it appears, and its text is labelled “AI-assisted”.

What makes it creative

  • The Opposite Trend Finder.
  • Four separate evidence answers instead of a single score.
  • A voice assistant that answers only from computed results.
  • A check that caught physically impossible values in the source data. For example, NASA POWER reports 191.77 mm/day of rain in southern Italy in February 2026; EarthPulse flags it as a likely data error because GPCP shows an ordinary month.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: missing data is never counted as zero. Model output is labelled as such. Correlation is never presented as cause. Unusual months are never called disasters.
  • Limits stated openly: EarthPulse samples about 1% of land, and most of its variables come from a single weather model.
  • Accessibility: colour is never the only signal, and charts have text descriptions.
  • Privacy: the microphone turns on only when pressed, and no audio is stored. No API keys are exposed in the browser.
  • Independence: EarthPulse is an independent project and is not affiliated with NASA.
